claims.text: Sliding friction mechanically disrupts or removes the initially protective passive oxide layer on the HEA.
Removal of the passive film exposes fresh alloy surface to the electrolyte.
The freshly exposed alloy surface is more susceptible to localized corrosion than the passivated surface.
Corrosion products, surface roughening, or loss of surface integrity accelerate subsequent wear.
Mutual amplification between passive-film removal, corrosion, and wear forms a positive feedback loop governing coupled tribo-corrosion degradation.
The HEA initially possesses a relatively stable passive oxide layer because of its corrosion resistance.
HEAs, including the cited refractory HEA examples, can exhibit high corrosion resistance.
The cited CrMoNbWV HEA exhibits both excellent wear performance and high electrochemical corrosion resistance in H2SO4 when these properties are tested separately.
An H2SO4 electrolyte is a relevant corrosive test environment for at least one cited refractory HEA.
Combined sliding and corrosion will produce greater total degradation than wear-only or corrosion-only exposure.
Wear volume will be greater under combined tribo-corrosion than under the wear-only baseline.
Corrosion damage will be greater under combined tribo-corrosion than under the static corrosion-only baseline.
The feedback loop will cause a nonlinear increase in degradation.
The predicted synergy should occur when the alloy forms a sufficiently robust passive film during corrosion-only exposure.
The prediction may fail when the oxide layer is inherently unstable.
The prediction may fail when sliding is too mild to disrupt the oxide significantly.
The magnitude of tribo-corrosion synergy depends on electrolyte concentration, sliding speed, load, and passive-film properties.
Chemical etching can produce an oxide-disrupted comparison surface, while pre-oxidation can produce a more stable-film comparison surface.
Enhancing or retaining the passive oxide layer should reduce both wear and corrosion contributions to synergistic degradation relative to an oxide-disrupted surface.
Profilometry, electrochemical testing, and XPS can respectively evaluate wear loss, corrosion response, and oxide-film condition in the proposed comparison.
